title: Text Filtering: sort, uniq, cut and tr
lead: Turn raw text into a useful report by sorting lines, counting duplicates, selecting fields and transforming characters.
objectives: Collapse or count consecutive duplicates with `uniq`.
Select fields from delimited text with `cut`.
Transform characters with `tr` and combine tools in pipelines.

sections.title: Sort lines with sort
body: `sort FILE` sorts lines alphabetically or lexically. `-r` reverses the order; `-n` sorts numeric values rather than text. For example, a plain text sort may place `100` before `2`.
`sort` prints its result and does not change the source file. Redirect the output to a different file if you want to keep the sorted result.

commands.where: When putting a list in alphabetical order.
When you want later values first.
commands.why: Produces the reverse of the same ordering.

commands.where: For files with one number per line.
commands.why: Places values such as `2` and `100` in numeric order.

sections.tip: By default, `sort` compares text. Use `-n` for numbers, and check the first lines with `head` if needed.

sections.title: Collapse duplicates with uniq
body: `uniq` collapses only identical adjacent lines. If duplicates occur in different parts of a file, sort them first to bring them together.
`uniq -c` prefixes each unique line with its count. This is useful for simple frequency reports.

commands.what: Collapses consecutive identical lines into one.
commands.where: When removing duplicates from a sorted list.
commands.why: Leaves one copy of each value.

commands.what: Collapses consecutive duplicates and prints their counts.
commands.where: When calculating how often each value occurs.
commands.why: Shows each value and its frequency together.

sections.warn: `uniq` does not search for duplicates across the whole file; it catches only adjacent repeats. The common pattern is `sort | uniq`.

sections.title: Select fields with cut and transform characters with tr
body: `cut -dDELIMITER -fFIELD` selects fields from delimited lines. CSV uses commas, while `/etc/passwd` uses colons. Select multiple fields with a comma-separated list such as `-f1,3`.

`tr SET1 SET2` transforms characters from standard input. For example, you can convert ASCII lowercase letters to uppercase. `cut`, `sort`, `uniq` and `tr` use stdin and stdout, so they can be combined with pipes.

commands.what: Selects the first field from comma-separated lines.
commands.where: When extracting a column from a CSV file.
commands.why: Removes columns you do not need.

commands.what: Selects the first and third fields.
commands.where: When you need more than one column.

commands.what: Converts ASCII lowercase letters to uppercase.
commands.where: When standardizing the letter case of text.

sections.tip: For text separated by variable amounts of whitespace, `awk` may be more flexible than `cut`; here we focus on fixed delimiters.

sections.title: Combine tools in a pipeline
body: Text filters are small and focused. For example, select a status-code field from a log, sort it and count it with `uniq -c`. Check the result on screen, then save it to a report with `>`.
Order matters: `sort | uniq -c` counts duplicates, then `sort -rn` sorts by count from highest to lowest.

commands.what: Counts values and sorts them from most to least frequent.
commands.where: When finding common values in logs or lists.
commands.why: Combines small tools into a report.

commands.what: Passes the selected field from CSV into a pipe.
commands.where: When preparing one column for another filter.
commands.why: Keeps each tool focused on one task.

sections.warn: `>` overwrites the existing contents of its target. Do not write over the source file; choose a separate report filename.

vm.intro: These filters only read input on your VM. Use separate filenames in your home directory for output reports.

v01.title: Numeric sort
v01.text: Sort the user IDs in `/etc/passwd` numerically and paste the first few lines.
differs: The IDs depend on the distribution; they should be in increasing numeric order.

v02.title: Select a CSV field
v02.text: Extract the name field from the report CSV in your home directory. If it is not present, replace the path with one of your CSV files.
differs: If your CSV uses a different delimiter, change `-d`. The first line may be a header.

v03.title: Count frequencies
v03.text: Count login shell fields in `/etc/passwd` and paste the frequency table.
differs: Counts vary by distribution. Make sure `sort` comes before `uniq -c`.

v04.title: Create a small report
v04.text: Prepare sample status codes in your home directory, sort and count them, then show the report.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab && printf '200
404
200
500
200
' > status.txt && sort status.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn > status_report.txt && cat status_report.txt

differs: If `status_report.txt` is empty, check `status.txt` and the redirection order. Do not overwrite the source.

q1.q: Which option sorts numeric lines by their numeric values?

q2.explain: Sorting brings identical values next to each other so `uniq` can collapse them.

q3.explain: `-d,` sets the delimiter to a comma and `-f2` selects the second field.

options: Converts lowercase ASCII letters to uppercase
q4.explain: `tr` transforms character sets; this example converts ASCII lowercase letters to uppercase.

summary: `sort` sorts text; use `sort -n` for numbers and `sort -r` for reverse order.
`uniq` collapses only adjacent duplicates, so sorting first is usually necessary.
`uniq -c` reports the count for each unique line.
`tr` transforms characters; combine small tools with pipes and write reports to separate files.

glossary.meaning: A command that reads input and writes selected or transformed output.
A character that separates fields in a line.
One column of a line split by a delimiter.
A list showing how often each value occurs.
